x1.h: Teaching it in class: your first two weeks with a new group
p: The first two weeks set the tone for two years. Use them to find out where students are and to show them what the course will feel like. In lesson 1, tell students in simple words what the exam is: three papers (Reading and Writing, Listening, Speaking), what each paper looks like, and how marks are earned. Show one real exercise from a past paper so that the exam does not feel like a mystery.

In lessons 2 to 4, run a short diagnostic of all four skills. For Reading, give one past-paper reading exercise. For Writing, ask for a 120 to 160 word email. For Listening, play one short extract with five multiple-choice questions. For Speaking, hold a five-minute conversation with each student, or with pairs, using everyday topics such as food, travel or technology. Do not give grades. Write a short note for each student: one strength, one need for each skill.

In lesson 5, give each student a one-page learner profile. It lists their four strengths and four needs and one goal for the term, written together with you. File it. Return to it every half term. Students who can see their own progress are more responsible and more engaged, which matches two of the Cambridge learner attributes.

b: Name and class. Date.
Reading: strength (finds facts quickly); need (misses implied meaning). Writing: strength (clear ideas); need (few linking words).
Listening: strength (gets names and numbers); need (loses track in long talks). Speaking: strength (fluent); need (short answers, little expansion).
Goal for this term: use three linking words in every piece of writing and expand every speaking answer with a reason and an example.

x1.h: Common difficulties for second-language learners, and what to do
p: Students in your class share a mother tongue or speak several languages at home. This is a strength, but it also shapes their English. Typical problems are: pronouncing sounds that do not exist in their home languages, using the wrong word stress, leaving out word endings such as -s and -ed, mixing up articles (a, an, the), and translating word for word from the home language so that a sentence sounds strange in English. Expect these errors. They are normal and they can be improved with practice.

Many students are also afraid of speaking in case they make mistakes. Build a classroom where mistakes are welcome. Praise the attempt first, correct one important error at a time, and use pair work so that students can try ideas in private before they speak to the class. Many students read slowly because they try to understand every word. Teach skimming, scanning and guessing from context so that they can cope with texts of 400 to 650 words in the time allowed.

Finally, students often write what they would say, not what the task needs. They forget the purpose, the reader and the format. This is why every writing lesson should start with three questions: Why am I writing? Who will read it? What type of text is it?

ex.t: Example: quick fixes you can use tomorrow
b: Word endings: ask students to underline every verb in their writing and check the ending.
Articles: collect ten sentences with a/an/the errors and let the class fix them together.
Stress: say words in a clap pattern (PHOto, phoTOgraphy) so students feel the stress.
Fear of speaking: use 30-second pair talks before any whole-class speaking.

x1.h: Teacher self-check: am I ready to start?
p: Use this list at the end of the unit. Tick what you can already do and plan how to learn the rest. You should be able to: explain the three papers and their marks to a parent in two minutes; name the sixteen skills (R1 to R4, W1 to W4, L1 to L4, S1 to S4); say when the exam series are and who the exams officer is; explain what a guided learning hour is and how many are planned; and say how Speaking is reported.

You should also know where the Cambridge papers, mark schemes and examiner reports are found and where the school's entry deadlines are published. If you cannot answer one of these questions, go back to the section above or ask your exams officer. A Cambridge teacher does not need to remember every number, but must know where to find it and must check it each year.

b: How many marks is Paper 1 and how long is it?
Which paper is marked by the teacher and checked by Cambridge?
Which grade scale is used for Speaking?
What are the guided learning hours?
Who can I ask about entries and access arrangements?

x2.h: Inclusion in the classroom, before any access arrangement
p: Access arrangements for the exam are only part of inclusion. Good teaching for all students starts in the classroom. Use clear fonts and enough space on handouts. Give instructions in short steps and both say them and write them. Check understanding by asking students to repeat the task in their own words. Seat students who find it hard to hear or see near the front. Give time to think before you ask for an answer. Allow quiet students to share ideas in writing or pairs first.

Remember the rule from Cambridge: an access arrangement should reflect the student's normal way of working at school. That means that if a student will need extra time or a reader in the exam, you must already be giving that kind of support in lessons and tests, and you must keep notes about it. Do not wait until the last month. Talk to your head of department, SENCO or exams officer at the start of the course. Keep a simple file for each student with the barrier, the support you give and the evidence.

b: Date, student, barrier seen (for example, slow reading speed).
Support used in class or test (extra reading time, large print).
Result (finished task, scores improved).
Who was told (parent, exams officer).

x2.h: Using results to improve your teaching
p: When results arrive, treat them as information, not as a verdict. Cambridge provides a Candidate Results Service, Results Analysis and Principal Examiner Reports for teachers. Use Results Analysis to compare how your students performed on each paper and each skill. Look for patterns: Was Listening much weaker than Reading? Did most students score low on the formal writing task? Did Speaking marks match your own internal marks?

Then make a plan. For each weak area choose one change and one date. For example: 'Add ten minutes of Exercise 3 listening every Monday' or 'Teach register in week 3 of next term and mark every Exercise 6 with the Content and Language tables'. Share the plan with your department and review it after the next set of mock exams. This is how teachers improve results year after year.

ex.t: Example: a results meeting in 30 minutes
b: 5 minutes: read the headline results for each paper.
10 minutes: find the weakest skill and the weakest exercise.
10 minutes: choose two teaching changes and who will do them.
5 minutes: write the actions and the review date in the department plan.

x2.h: Talking to students and parents about grades
p: Parents and students often ask, 'What does this grade mean?' Prepare a short, honest answer. A* to C means students are well prepared for a wide range of courses. Grade C overall with Speaking grade 2 can be seen as roughly B2 on the CEFR. Cambridge IGCSEs are accepted by leading universities and employers. Never promise a grade. Say what the student can do now and what must improve to reach the next step.

Use simple language and examples. For example: 'Tolu is very good at finding facts in a text, but she loses marks in the formal writing task because her paragraphs are not linked. If she practises linking words and writes one practice review every week, she can improve.' Always end with an action that the student and the parent can help with.

ex.t: Example: a three-sentence report to parents
b: Strength: reads and listens well, gets most multiple-choice items right.
Need: writing lacks detail and organisation, which affects the Language mark.
Next step: one 120 to 160 word practice text each week, marked with the Content and Language tables.

x3.h: The sixteen skills in plain classroom words
p: Turn each assessment objective into a sentence that students understand. Reading. R1: I can find the facts the text gives me. R2: I can see how ideas, opinions and feelings connect (for example, because, but, so). R3: I can choose the right details for a purpose. R4: I can understand what the writer means but does not say. Writing. W1: I can give facts, ideas and opinions clearly. W2: I can put ideas in order and join them with linking words. W3: I can use a range of grammar and vocabulary. W4: I can write in the right style for the reader.

Listening. L1: I can catch specific information such as names, times and places. L2: I can understand what speakers think and feel. L3: I can follow how their ideas link. L4: I can understand what is hinted but not said. Speaking. S1: I can talk about ideas, facts and opinions. S2: I can use a range of words and grammar and control them. S3: I can develop my answers and keep the conversation going. S4: I can say words clearly and use stress and intonation to show meaning.

Print this list for your students. Ask them to colour each skill green, yellow or red every month. Seeing the skills as small, learnable abilities helps students feel that the exam can be improved step by step.

b: Put the sixteen 'I can' sentences on the classroom wall.
After a task, students write the skill code on a sticky note to show which skill they practised.
Review the wall each month: which skills have many notes and which have none?

x3.h: Weightings and how they should shape your teaching time
p: Reading is 35 per cent of the written grade, Writing 35 per cent and Listening 30 per cent. Speaking is separately endorsed, but it is a compulsory component. If you have about 130 hours, a rough guide for planning might be: about 45 hours for Reading skills, about 45 hours for Writing, about 40 hours for Listening, and speaking practice built into almost every lesson. This is only a guide. Adjust it to your students' needs.

Remember that Writing earns its marks from two things at once: Content (6) and Language (9) in each task. A student who writes a relevant but simple text may earn most of the Content marks and few of the Language marks. This is why you should plan regular practice in vocabulary range, sentence variety and linking, not only in 'what to write'. In Reading and Listening, remember that every question is worth one mark, so students should answer every question and not leave blanks.

ex.t: Example: a term plan using the weightings
b: Weeks 1 to 4: reading skills (skim, scan, careful reading) plus paragraph linking in writing.
Weeks 5 to 8: listening exercises 1 and 2 plus informal email writing.
Weeks 9 to 12: listening exercises 3 to 5 plus review writing and a speaking mock.

p: 'Speaking does not count.' Speaking does not change the written grade, but it is a separate result on the certificate and it is compulsory. Employers and universities read it, so teach it seriously. 'The exam is only about grammar.' The exam tests how well students understand and communicate in English, not how well they recite rules. 'More words get more marks.' Writing tasks are marked for relevance, development and control of language, not length. Students who go far above the word range can lose control and accuracy.

'We can use any old past paper.' Always use papers for the right syllabus and the right year, and check the Changes section. The 2024 to 2026 syllabus removed tiers, replaced the summary task with a multiple-choice question, made Listening 100 per cent multiple choice, and increased the Speaking marks from 30 to 40. Older papers may not match. 'Any dictionary can be used.' Dictionaries are not allowed in Paper 1 or Paper 3.

ex.t: Example: myth or fact? A staff meeting game
b: Read each statement above aloud.
Teachers vote 'myth' or 'fact' with coloured cards.
Check the syllabus pages together and discuss why the myth is attractive.

x4.h: Phrase banks you can give to your students
p: Students need a toolbox of language. Use the lists in the syllabus as a base. Linking words for cause and effect: therefore, because of, as a result, consequently. For addition: in addition, moreover, furthermore, as well as. For contrast and concession: however, in contrast, whereas, although. For time and sequence in speaking: at the start of, first of all, finally. Other discourse markers: that's why, on top of that, plus, having said that.

Expansion phrases from the speaking content: to give examples, 'just to name a few'; to give a reason, 'and that is why'; to compare, 'just like', 'while'; to speculate, 'I suppose'; to clarify, 'Sorry, when you said ..., did you mean ...?' and 'Sorry, I didn't quite catch that.' Add useful phrases for opinions (in my opinion, personally), agreeing and disagreeing (I see what you mean, but ...), advantages and disadvantages, and predictions (I think it will ...).

Print the phrase bank, but do not let students simply copy it. Ask them to use at least three new phrases in each writing task and each speaking practice, and to highlight them. Over time, students move these phrases from the page into their own natural language.

b: Basic: 'I like swimming. It is good for health.'
Better: 'I like swimming because it keeps me fit. In addition, it helps me relax.'
Best: 'Although I do not have much free time, I try to swim twice a week, because it keeps me fit. In addition, it helps me relax after school.'

x4.h: Teaching vocabulary and grammar for range and accuracy
p: The Language marks reward range and accuracy. Teach vocabulary in groups, not in long lists: words that go together (collocations such as 'make a decision', 'do research'), phrasal verbs (take up, look into, find out), set phrases and a few idioms, and synonyms to avoid repeating the same word. Teach each new item with a sentence, a sentence of the student's own, and a short speaking use. Keep a class 'word wall' by topic: environment, health, food, film, travel, technology, celebrations, science, arts and shopping.

For grammar, teach a range of verb forms and tenses, conditional forms and a variety of sentence structures. Teach them through use: show a short model text, ask students to find the structure, practise it in a controlled task, then use it in a free task. For example, teach the first conditional through a short talk about an event ('If the weather is bad, we will ...') and then use it in an informal email. Mark the structure, not only the error, so that students learn what to aim for.

b: Show five new words on the board with a picture or example.
Students write one true sentence with each word.
Pairs swap and correct each other's sentences.
Next lesson, start with a quick quiz and use two of the words in a speaking task.

x4.h: A weekly timetable that builds all four skills
p: It is easy to teach only what feels comfortable. A weekly timetable stops this. If you have about four lessons a week, you might plan: Lesson 1 Reading (a short text, strategy practice, then marking), Lesson 2 Writing (plan, draft, check, with a model), Lesson 3 Listening (before-during-after, with transcript review), Lesson 4 Speaking and language (pair and group work, pronunciation, vocabulary and grammar).

Add short routines to every lesson: five minutes of vocabulary at the start, two minutes of pronunciation, and a one-minute reflection at the end ('What did I learn? What do I still find hard?'). Once a month, do a full past-paper exercise under timed conditions. Every half term, carry out a short mock of one paper. Keep a record of marks so that you can see progress.

b: Mon: Reading, skim and scan an article, then Exercise 1 style questions.
Tue: Writing, plan and write an informal email, peer-check for linking words.
Thu: Listening, Exercise 2 style extracts, check with the transcript.
Fri: Speaking, short talks in pairs, then feedback on one pronunciation point.

p: Share these strategies with students, and let them adapt them. Exercise 1 (8 marks, short answers): read the questions first; underline the question word; scan for the answer; write a few words, not a sentence. Exercise 2 (9 marks, matching): read the statements first, then read each text and mark clues; remember each letter can be used more than once; look for the idea, not the same words. Exercise 3 (7 marks, notes): look at the headings; find the right part of the text; write short notes in your own or the text's words; do not put an answer under the wrong heading.

Exercise 4 (6 marks, multiple choice): read the question, find the part of the text, then test each option; rule out options that use the same words but change the meaning. Exercise 5 (15 marks, informal email): underline purpose, reader and prompts; plan three paragraphs; use a friendly style; give details; check linking words and verb forms. Exercise 6 (15 marks, formal text): same steps but with a more formal style, a clear opening and closing, and a structure suited to the text type (review, report, essay or article).

ex.t: Example: a time plan for the 2 hours (suggestion, not an official rule)
b: About 60 minutes for the four reading exercises (60 marks across the paper means about 2 minutes per mark).
About 25 minutes for each writing task, including planning and checking.
Keep 5 to 10 minutes for a final check of all answers. Practise this plan in mocks and adjust it for each student.

p: Paper 2 is about 50 minutes and includes 6 minutes to copy answers onto the answer sheet. Teach students to use any time given before each exercise to read the questions and guess what kind of information they will hear. In Exercise 1 the options are pictures, so students should look at the differences between pictures. In Exercises 2, 3 and 5 the options are written, so students should underline the key words in each option. In Exercise 4, students must match speakers to eight statements, with two statements not used, so they should cross out each statement after using it.

Because each recording plays twice, advise students to answer on the first listening and check on the second. They must answer every question, since a blank earns no mark. Teach them to listen for opinion words such as 'I'd rather', 'unfortunately', 'actually', 'in fact' and for linking words such as 'but', 'so' and 'although', which often show the real answer. At the end, they should transfer answers carefully: copy the right letter to the right question number.

ex.t: Example: a classroom routine for listening
b: Predict: read the questions and guess the type of answer.
Listen once: answer what you are sure of.
Listen twice: check and fill gaps.
Review: replay the extract with the transcript and underline the words that gave the answer.

x5.h: Paper 3 Speaking: what students need to know
p: Prepare students for the whole test. After a short warm-up they will answer questions in Part 1 (interview), give a short talk in Part 2, and discuss related questions in Part 3. In Part 2 they have up to one minute to read the card and prepare, but they may not write notes. Teach them to use the minute to choose three ideas in their head, to decide how to start, and to think of one example.

Teach them to keep talking: use expansion (give a reason and an example), paraphrase if they forget a word, and use phrases such as 'Sorry, could you say that again?' if they do not understand. Practise often with a timer. Record students and let them listen to themselves. This helps with pronunciation and intonation, which together carry 10 of the 40 marks.

b: Second 0 to 10: read the card, find the topic and the three bullet points.
Second 10 to 40: think of one idea and one example for each point.
Second 40 to 60: think of an opening sentence and a closing sentence.
Then speak for the time allowed, without notes.
